## Color Track

Spectral rendering techniques to improve colour matching in virtual production

Presenter: Vlad Simion


## Who am I?

- Graduated RIT's Munsell Color Science Lab, with a Master's degree in Colo(u)r Science
- Color Scientist for Seismiq, handling many aspects of R&D for projects in entertainment, live events, and motion pictures



## What problem?


Both charts lit by the same light at 6500K (left) and 3200K (right). Both charts were simulated using RGB rendering.


## More practically



## But first, some CG background!

- All of the backdrops are rendered in real time using rendering engines that compute light-matter interaction in RGB terms.
- These RGB values often come from what an artist thought something should look like or potentially objects measured in very controlled and specific environments.


## In more color science terms



## Some more CG background!

- The rendering equation! Notice how there aren't actual units. But it mostly gets assigned RGB values!
- In fact, most rendering software (and hardware) is highly optimized to work with triplets.



## But what if we want to move away from RGB?

- Well, it turns out some have tried this since as early as the 80's. But it has not gained a lot of traction, and it still does not happen in real-time rendering engines.
- We could speculate that complexity and 'RGB looks good enough' have deterred people from pursuing real -time implementations.


## Even in 1999 spectral rendering was a hot topic!



## Optimizations first!

- We need to remember that there are two steps in rendering: storing the material/light 'color' and transporting the 'color' of the ray throughout the scene.
- Fully Spectral Rendering would mean 401 terms in our equations! Maybe a bit too many! But what if we can reduce it fewer?


## Fewer terms

- Looking at historical papers, six dimensionality reduction methods seem to keep appearing:
- -RGB
- -Fully Spectral (every 1 nm)
- -Monte Carlo (each ray gets assigned a wavelength)
- -Binning (similar to Fully Spectral, just ever X nm)
- -PCA (we run Principal Component Analysis on the scene and only preserve the first six terms)
- -Polynomial (each spectrum becomes a list of polynomial coefficients)


## So how did we choose the number of variables?






## How can we demonstrate that spectral rendering would even be better?

- Devise an experiment that revolves around virtual production (VP).
- Use spectral rendering techniques to display scenes.
- Look at the difference between displayed and measured scenes from the perspective of a camera.


## We need a scene!

- Chose four test grids, with multiple samples present, and four lights each measured at 3200k and at 6500k.

- Yes, but no.
- There are advantages and disadvantages.
- Choosing the number of variables is very important. If we made the bins larger, we would lose accuracy and gain performance; it would be the same if we used fewer polynomial terms. In general we choose what felt good for the trade-offs in our case.

## Can we rank them?


## Are there errors in our ways?

- Probably!
- The camera-to-wall calibration will never be perfect. The camera does not fulfill the Luther-Ives condition either. We also have to use RGB as the transport mechanism between the rendered image and the wall. In short, plenty of sources of error.



## But did we achieve what we wanted in this research?

- In short… yes!
- We showed that we could reduce deltaE if we used spectral rendering.
- I hope that the industry can take notice of this and start thinking of ways to actually implement these methods. This also opens the door to using different observers in rendering engines to help further VFX work.
- Using methods that can compress spectral data helps reduce complexity, albeit at the cost of accuracy. More research is needed to determine the best trade-off. Maybe even combining methods would improve accuracy.


## Thank you!

## Advancing Color Science

## Optimizing Color Grading with the Gamut Rings Color Scope

Presenter: Kenichiro Masaoka

Japan Broadcasting Corporation (NHK) / NHK Foundation










## From CIEXYZ to CIELAB

## LMS Cones

- Distinct spectral sensitivities
- Underlie the physiological basis of color perception

## 1905: Munsell Color Order System

- Hue, value (lightness), and chroma
- Designed for perceptual uniformity
- Not colorimetric

## 1931: CIE Basic Colorimetry

- Tristimulus values ( X , Y , Z ) based on CMFs
- ( x , y ) chromaticity diagram
- Constructed for practical color reproduction
- Lacks perceptual uniformity



## 1940s -1970s: Toward Unifying Munsell and CIEXYZ 1976: CIE ( L *, a *, b *)

- International standard, formalizing Munsell's principles
- Lightness ( L *), chroma ( C *), and hue angle ( h )
- Perceptually uniform
- Wrong chromatic adaptation transform (CAT) works only when adapted to a white close to D65

```
L * = 116 f ( Y / Y n ) - 16 a * = 500 [ f ( X / X n ) -f ( Y / Y n )] b * = 200 [ f ( Y / Y n ) -f ( Z / Z n )] f ( t ): cube-root-like lightness scaling
```



## Chromaticity Gamut vs Color Gamut



- RGB triangle areas are often called 'color gamut'
- However, xy and u′v′ areas are not proportional
- u′v′ space is nominally more uniform than xy space
- MacAdam ellipses (MacAdam, JOSA, 1942)
- Sparsely sampled at 10 × JND scale from one observer
- Low reproducibility (Wyszecki & Stiles, Color Science , 1982)
- Chromaticity density maps based on CIEDE2000 (Masaoka, JSID, 2025)
- Neither xy nor u′v′ is uniform
- Chromaticity diagrams lack a luminance or lightness axis, limiting their ability to fully represent perceptual color differences
- Chromaticity Gamut ≠ Color Gamut








## Standardized CIELAB Gamut Metric

- The color gamut of a display is described as a 3D range in the D50 CIELAB space (SID/ICDM, CIE, IEC)
- The wrong CAT is replaced with the Bradford CAT
- D50 CIELAB is also used in ICC profiles as a standard PCS for device-independent color conversion
- However, visualization is challenging, as static 3D views make it difficult to interpret how chroma varies with hue angles and lightness









Even though we navigate daily through a perceptual world of three spatial dimensions and reason occasionally about higher  dimensional  arenas  with  mathematical  ease,  the world portrayed on our information displays is caught up in the two-dimensionality of the endless flatlands of paper and video screen.

All  communication between the readers of an image and the  makers  of  an  image  must  now  take  place  on  a  twodimensional surface. Escaping this flatland is the essential task  of  envisioning  information -for  all  the  interesting worlds  (physical,  biological,  imaginary,  human)  that  we seek to understand are inevitably and happily multivariate in nature. Not flatlands.

(Tufte, Envisioning Information, 1990)



## Gamut Rings: 2D Visualization of Color Gamut

- Unwrap the CIELAB gamut into concentric rings in a 2D diagram
- Arranged in polar coordinates, preserving hue angle
- Ring areas are proportional to gamut volume
- 10 concentric rings, each spanning 10-unit lightness range
- Lightness increases from near-black inner ring to near-white outer ring
- Hue angle is preserved in polar coordinates
- Chroma is radial distance from the inner side of each ring







## In 2021, Gamut Rings were standardized in

- SID/ICDM:2021 Information Display Measurement Standard (IDMS) v1.1
- CIE 246:2021 Colour Gamuts for Output Media
- IEC 62977-2-1:2021 Electronic Displays -Part 2-1: Measurements of Optical Characteristics -Fundamental Measurements



## Portrait Displays Adds Gamut Rings Support in Calman (August 2024)




## RTINGS.com's Test Bench 2.0 Adopts Gamut Rings (March 2025)

## 'Color Gamut

The color gamut test has been removed completely, as the 2D chromaticity plots much of the industry uses are no longer considered to be a valid way to measure chromaticity. Gamut rings have replaced this test .' chromaticity color gamut

## 2. Color Scopes for Color Grading





## RGB cube

- Signal domain representation
- Basis for scope transformations


## YCbCr space

- Affine transform of RGB cube
- Hue angle and saturation represented in polar form
- Hexagonal Cb -Cr boundary


## Yxy space

- Shows chromaticity gamut boundary (RGB triangle)



## Gamut Rings Color Scope

- Motivation: Conventional scopes lack perceptual uniformity
- Ring scope enables simultaneous monitoring of lightness, chroma, and hue angle in a perceptually uniform 2D layout
- Reference space: D65 CIELAB, anchored to the input signal's white





## Mapping Internal Color Samples onto Rings

- During the stabilization of the slanted gamut pieces along the L * axis, scale each internal color sample ( C *) relative to the boundaries of its L * -h plane
- Flatten each piece while preserving the relative chroma positions of all internal samples




## LUT-Based Implementation

- Rasterize the rings (e.g., 600 × 600 pixels)
- Generate a LUT mapping all RGB codes to pixel indices (256 3 entries for 8-bit RGB)
- During visualization, each input pixel is moved to its LUT-designated ring location
- Implemented in MATLAB (achieved ~15 fps at 720p HD input on a typical consumer laptop without explicit GPU programming)
- DirectShow-device support






## 3. Demonstration



## Overview


- Mid-tone gradations in the sky are distinguishable


- Overlaps high-lightness colors, making mid-tones harder to distinguish
- Chromaticities near black are widely scattered


- Plots hue angle and saturation
- Gradations are compressed and near-black colors are often invisible




## Ring Scope -Gain

- As lightness decreases, the color distribution shifts from the outer rings toward the inner rings, while hue angles remain unchanged






## Ring Scope -Saturation

- Distributions in each ring collapse toward its inner boundary when desaturated







- Distribution remains unaffected by gain, as expected






## Vectorscope -Gain and Saturation

- Distribution contracts when either gain or saturation is reduced, indicating that changes in these two parameters cannot be distinguished solely with this scope

## HDR Applications of Ring Scope

- Challenge: CIELAB defines lightness up to L * = 100; HDR exceeds this range
- Solution: Variable L * setting (e.g. 203 nits) and extra rings beyond L * = 100 (e.g., for Highlights/Specular/Signal Extension)
- Implementation Example:
- -FF Pictures + NHK: HDR Gamut Rings Signal Monitor (IBC 2023)
- -4K HDR real-time rendering
- -Standalone software and plug-in for Davinci Resolve
- Benefits:
- -More accurate HDR grading and headroom visualization
- -Real-time compliance checks (e.g., DCI-P3 within BT.2020)
- -Shared visual Q/C reference for directors and colorists



## Trial Application in NHK Program Production

- Ring Scope used in pre-shoot look tests for NHK's morning drama, involving direction, art, and technical teams
- To check colors in costumes, makeup, and sets, refining and sharing the overall color plan

## Next Steps

- Implementation across the entire production workflow, from pre- through post-production
- Promoting the Ring Scope as a visualization tool shared between creative and technical teams



## Exploring Alternative Color Spaces

## CIELAB (Bradford CAT)

- Widely adopted (SID/ICDM, IEC, CIE, ICC PCS)
- Limitations: non-uniformity, artifacts in certain regions

## Alternatives

- CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022): ongoing CIE work on perceptual spaces
- •
- ICtCp (BT.2100): optimized for HDR & WCG video encoding Note: CIE standard color spaces and ICtCp employ different chromatic adaptation models, and therefore cannot be directly compared

## Opportunity

- Gamut Rings with alternative spaces can provide practical feedback on perceptual validity

## Conclusion

- Gamut Rings Color Scope provides a unified view of lightness, chroma, and hue angle in a perceptually uniform layout
- Compared to chromaticity and vectorscopes, it reveals more meaningful color structures
- Lightweight implementation enables real-time operation, making it practical for use in interactive color grading environments
- The perceptually intuitive visualization is expected to facilitate more efficient and effective color grading with smoother communication between colorists and directors

reference:
The historical development of CIE color spaces began with the 1931 CIE Basic Colorimetry, which defined tristimulus values (X, Y, Z) based on CMFs and introduced the (x, y) chromaticity diagram. This system was constructed for practical color reproduction but notably lacked perceptual uniformity. Progressing towards better perceptual representation, the 1976 CIE (L*, a*, b*) system, also known as CIELAB, was established as an international standard. It formalized Munsell's principles by defining lightness (L*), chroma (C*), and hue angle (h), and was designed to be perceptually uniform, though its initial chromatic adaptation transform (CAT) worked only when adapted to a white close to D65. 

In modern color management, the color gamut of a display is described as a 3D range in the D50 CIELAB space, where the original CAT is replaced with the Bradford CAT. D50 CIELAB is also used in ICC profiles as a standard PCS for device-independent color conversion. The Gamut Rings Color Scope, which provides a unified view of lightness, chroma, and hue angle in a perceptually uniform 2D layout, utilizes D65 CIELAB as its reference space, anchored to the input signal's white. The generation of D65 Gamut Rings for color scope involves computing the gamut boundary at constant lightness levels in the D65 CIELAB space, requiring conversion from CIE 1931 (Y, x, y) to CIELAB coordinates. Gamut Rings themselves were standardized in CIE 246:2021 Colour Gamuts for Output Media. While CIELAB (with Bradford CAT) is widely adopted, it still has limitations such as non-uniformity and artifacts in certain regions. Ongoing CIE work on perceptual spaces includes alternatives like CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022), though it is important to note that CIE standard color spaces and ICtCp employ different chromatic adaptation models and therefore cannot be directly compared.
